editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech spends a long time on two closures from a generation ago, Ravenscraig and the Leigh pits. The charge it makes is about process: the decisions were taken hundreds of miles away, and nobody asked the communities what should come next.

That charge is fair, and it gives the Prime Minister a test he can be held to. The places now facing the same kind of decision are Aberdeen, as North Sea production declines, and the Grangemouth site. On Aberdeen the speech offers only 'more to say in due course.' On Grangemouth it offers continued effort to 'help secure' new investment. Whether these places are asked what comes next, before rather than after the jobs go, will show whether the lessons of Ravenscraig were learned.

The figures he cites show how long deindustrialisation keeps doing harm. They include one in five empty shops in Dundee against one in twenty in Edinburgh, and a shrinking working population in Inverclyde. They also include a seven-year gap in male life expectancy over ten miles, and one in six young people not in education, employment or training. These are compound effects built up over thirty years. The concrete offers set against them are modest: a £10 million defence college fund matched by Holyrood, a share of a UK-wide £1 billion research pot, and devolved employability funding. Those offers are the right kind of tool, but they are small next to the scale of the damage.

The one item with real constitutional weight is the offer of DWP devolution, meaning localised employment support shaped by Holyrood. That would move part of the welfare system across the border, something that has long been one of the most guarded powers at Westminster. It is attached to an 'Easterhouse principle' that asks Holyrood to devolve further in turn. The offer may therefore be judged less on its merits than on whether Edinburgh accepts the conditions that come with it.

There is also an irony in the speech's list of Scottish achievements. Public ownership of rail is among the things the Prime Minister applauds, and Scotland brought ScotRail into public hands before Great British Railways had even chosen its headquarters. On that question Holyrood was ahead of Westminster, not lagging behind it. That weakens the framing of Scotland as the place that now needs to catch up on handing power down.
